notes.title: Start here: learning OpenStatus by reading its tests
notes.body:
OpenStatus is an open-source uptime monitor with public status pages. This checkout is the monorepo itself, with a study library in `docs/`. This quest uses the **test-first learning lab**: `docs/test-first-learning-lab/`. Its idea is that a test is the most precise description of what code does, so you learn a module by reading its tests and then writing the next one.

Read in order:

1. `01-test-map.md`: which kinds of tests exist and where.
2. `02-service-test-workouts.md`: status reports in `packages/services`.
3. `03-router-test-workouts.md`: the same feature through the tRPC routers in `packages/api`.
4. `04-public-page-and-utils-tests.md`: the public status page helpers and the SSRF guard in `packages/utils`.

The workouts mix real test excerpts with code marked *illustrative fake*. Always open the real file a workout cites and check the behaviour yourself.

notes.title: Concept: status reports, from service verb to router
notes.body:
A **status report** is a public incident write-up on a status page, with a series of updates. The service verbs live in `packages/services/src/status-report/`; the tRPC routers in `packages/api/src/router/` wrap them and translate their errors.

Read `create.ts` and list every step in order: the scope check, input parsing, the page lookup (note its `where`), the page-component validation, and the check that compares the components' page with the requested page. For each failure, note which error class is thrown. Then read `notify.ts` and list its early returns and their conditions.

Next, open `packages/api/src/router/statusReport.ts`:

- For `create`, note what the procedure returns and how it handles errors (follow `toTRPCError` into `service-adapter.ts`).
- For `list`, compare the zod input object with the object passed to `listStatusReports`. Then read `list.ts` to see how each field is used.

Finally, re-read workout 1 of the service file and the real test it cites to see which rows one create writes.

notes.title: Concept: building the public timeline, and guarding URLs
notes.body:
The public status page shows a timeline of **events**: maintenances, incidents and status reports. `getEvents` in `packages/api/src/router/statusPage.utils.ts` builds that list. Read it slowly and make a table with one row per source (maintenances, incidents, reports) and these columns: how it is filtered by component or monitor, whether the 45-day threshold applies, and what `type`, `status` and `to` the event gets. Fill it in from the code, not from the workout's bullet list.

In `packages/api/src/router/statusPage.ts`, find where `statusReports` is sorted. A JavaScript comparator must return a negative number when `a` comes first, a positive number when `b` comes first, and zero for a tie, and it must be consistent. Check each branch of this comparator against that contract.

The SSRF guard in `packages/utils/src/ssrf.ts` stops the server from fetching internal addresses. Read `isBlockedIPv4`, `isBlockedIPv6`, `isBlockedHost`, and both `assertSafeUrl` functions. For each, list exactly what it inspects and what it ignores.

excerpts.quote: `getEvents` collects maintenances, incidents, and reports into a common event shape

notes.title: Why components from another page cause a conflict
notes.body:
`createStatusReport` first loads the page by id and workspace, then calls `validatePageComponentIds`, which checks the ids against the workspace and reports which page they belong to. If that page is not null and differs from `input.pageId`, the service throws `ConflictError` naming both pages. The components are legitimately the workspace's own, so this is a conflict between two inputs, not an ownership failure.

- *NotFoundError*: the page itself was found; the components are validated by workspace.
- *ForbiddenError*: the components belong to the same workspace.
- *Linked anyway*: the throw happens before the insert.

excerpts.quote: if (validated.pageId !== null && validated.pageId !== input.pageId) { throw new ConflictError(

notes.title: Why a foreign page id surfaces as NOT_FOUND
notes.body:
The page lookup filters on both `page.id` and `page.workspaceId`, so a page from another workspace is not found, and the service throws `NotFoundError("page", input.pageId)`. The router catches it and calls `toTRPCError`, which maps a ServiceError with code `NOT_FOUND` to a `TRPCError` with code `NOT_FOUND`. The router test asserts exactly this code.

- *FORBIDDEN*: the service never reveals that the page exists elsewhere.
- *BAD_REQUEST*: the page id is a valid number, so input parsing passes.
- *INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR*: the service throws before any insert.

notes.title: Why notifying on a plan without subscribers does nothing
notes.body:
After loading the update and checking that it belongs to the caller's workspace, `notifyStatusReport` tests `ctx.workspace.limits["status-subscribers"]`. When it is false, the function simply returns: no dispatch, no error. The comment says this silent skip matches the existing email router. The workout asks whether that should be user-visible instead.

- *ForbiddenError*: that is thrown only when the update belongs to another workspace.
- *Dispatches anyway*: the plan check runs before `dispatchStatusReportUpdate`.
- *Queued for later*: there is no queue; the call just ends.

notes.title: Why a statuses filter on the tRPC list has no effect
notes.body:
The router's input is `z.object({ period, order, pageId })`. A zod object schema strips keys it does not declare unless told otherwise, so `statuses` disappears during parsing. The router then always calls the service with `statuses: []`, `limit: 10_000` and `offset: 0`. In `listStatusReports` a status condition is added only when `input.statuses.length > 0`, so every status comes back. The workout predicts this test would fail today.

- *Only resolved*: the service supports the filter, but the router never passes it.
- *Zod throws*: an object schema strips unknown keys by default.
- *Capped at 100*: that limit belongs to the separate Connect handler; tRPC passes 10,000.

notes.title: Why pageComponentId wins over monitorId
notes.body:
The maintenance filter checks `if (pageComponentId)` first and returns its match. Only when `pageComponentId` is falsy does it try `monitorId`, and when neither is given it keeps every maintenance. The comment calls monitorId the backward-compatibility fallback. The reports filter uses the same order.

- *monitorId alone*: it is the fallback, not the first choice.
- *Either one*: the branches return before the next is tried, so there is no OR.
- *Both at once*: there is no AND either.

excerpts.quote: prioritize pageComponentId, fallback to monitorId for backward compatibility

notes.title: Why static components show no incidents
notes.body:
All incident handling sits inside `if (componentType !== "static") { ... }`. A static component is a manual entry on the page with no monitor behind it, so the code skips incidents entirely, whatever monitor id is passed. The monitor filter and the 45-day threshold apply only inside that block.

- *All incidents from 45 days*: that is the behaviour for monitor-type components.
- *Only unresolved ones*: the block is skipped as a whole.
- *Only matching monitorId*: the filter never runs for a static component.

notes.title: Why a monitoring update closes the range but stays degraded
notes.body:
`getEvents` sorts a report's updates by date. If `report.status` is `"resolved"` it emits a `success` event. Otherwise it emits a `degraded` event whose `to` is the last update's date when that update's status is `resolved` or `monitoring`, and `null` otherwise. Here the report is investigating and the last update is monitoring, so the event is degraded and ends at that update.

- *Success*: only the report's own status `resolved` gives success.
- *Open with to null*: monitoring is one of the two statuses that set `to`.
- *No event*: unresolved reports are always included when they have updates.

notes.title: Why the old report stays but the old maintenance goes
notes.body:
`pastThreshod` is today minus `pastDays`. The maintenance loop returns early when `maintenance.from < pastThreshod`, and incidents check `createdAt` the same way. The reports branch has no such check; its comment says all unresolved reports are displayed. So a 60-day-old maintenance is dropped while a 60-day-old unresolved report stays on the timeline.

- *Both*: the maintenance threshold drops the old maintenance.
- *Neither*: reports are deliberately exempt from the threshold.
- *Only the maintenance*: it is the other way round.

excerpts.quote: we don't check threshold here because we display all unresolved reports

notes.title: Why the report comparator is inconsistent
notes.body:
A comparator returns a negative number to put `a` first and a positive number to put `b` first. This one returns `-1` when `a` has no updates (correct: a goes first) and also `-1` when `b` has no updates, which again puts `a` first, the opposite of the comment's intent. The second branch should return `1`. Because the result depends on argument order, the comparator is inconsistent, and the final order depends on the engine's sort algorithm.

- *Returns 0*: 0 is returned only when both have no updates.
- *Throws*: the empty-array checks return before the last-update read.
- *Puts the empty report first*: -1 orders `a`, not `b`, first.

notes.title: Why the hex IPv4-mapped loopback is blocked
notes.body:
`isBlockedHost` sees a bracketed host and calls `isBlockedIPv6` with `::ffff:7f00:1`. That function handles the `::ffff:` prefix: it first tries the rest as a dotted IPv4, then splits the two hex groups `7f00` and `1`, rebuilds `127.0.0.1` from their bytes, and asks `isBlockedIPv4`, which blocks the 127 range. The comment explains why: Node's URL parser rewrites the dotted form into this hex form.

- *Only the dotted form*: the hex branch exists for exactly this input.
- *Every IPv6 literal*: public IPv6 addresses are allowed.
- *IPv6 skips the checks*: bracketed hosts go through `isBlockedIPv6`.

excerpts.quote: Node's URL parser converts ::ffff:127.0.0.1 to ::ffff:7f00:1 (hex form)

notes.title: Why a hostname pointing at a private IP passes
notes.body:
Read the body of `assertSafeUrl`: it parses the URL, rejects non-HTTP protocols, and calls `isBlockedHost(parsed.hostname)`. `isBlockedHost` compares the name with a blocklist and checks it only if it is a raw IP literal. Nothing calls a DNS resolver, so a public-looking name whose record points to `10.0.0.5` passes. The docblock and the test section header both claim DNS resolution; the code does not do it, and the tests only use literal hosts.

- *Blocked after a lookup*: no lookup happens.
- *An allowlist*: the guard uses blocklists, not an allowlist.
- *Invalid URL*: the URL parses fine; only parsing failures throw that.

notes.title: Which rows one status-report create writes
notes.body:
Workout 1 lists the happy-path effects of `createStatusReport`: a `status_report` row, a `status_report_update` row (the initial update), a `status_report_to_page_component` row linking the affected component, and audit rows for both the report and the update. The audit rows are written with `emitAudit` inside the same transaction.

- *Update row only, audit later*: the link row is also written, and audit is not deferred.
- *Link row and one audit row*: both the report and the update are audited.
- *Subscriber notification rows*: notifying subscribers is the separate `notifyStatusReport` verb.

excerpts.quote: status_report_to_page_component row audit rows for report and update
